## Chapter Summary

A query is a written request for data that the database answers where the data is stored. Querying suits an accounting analysis when the data is large, when it spans related tables, and when the procedure must be repeated. The query text itself documents what was extracted, so it can be reviewed and run again. SQL is the standard language of relational databases, and it is declarative: you state the result you want, and the database decides how to produce it. This book uses SQLite, which keeps a whole database in one file, and DB Browser for SQLite, whose Database Structure tab shows every table and column and whose Execute SQL tab runs queries. Because DB Browser can change a database as well as read it, you work in a copy of the download, CharlesRiver_Work.sqlite.

A SELECT statement names the columns it wants and the table they come from. Aliases rename columns in the result, and calculated columns apply arithmetic to each row, with ROUND keeping amounts to the cent. DISTINCT lists the values a column actually holds, which is the way to learn the valid values before you filter on one. The WHERE clause keeps the rows that meet a condition, built from comparison operators, BETWEEN, IN, and LIKE, and combined with AND, OR, and NOT. Text values sit in single quotes and must match the data exactly. Dates stored as text are compared with dates written the same way. Parentheses make the order of AND and OR explicit. A missing value is NULL, which no comparison can match, so IS NULL and IS NOT NULL are the tests for it.

ORDER BY sorts a result by one or more columns, and LIMIT keeps its first rows. Together they rank transactions, such as the largest variances of a year. A script saved from the Execute SQL tab keeps a chapter's queries together, with a header comment that records their purpose, source, preparer, and checks. Syntax errors stop a query with a message. Logical errors, such as a missing comma or a missing pair of parentheses, return a result that answers the wrong question, and the defense against them is to know what the result should look like before running the query.

Applied to the controller's question, the queries showed that the manufacturing variance is recorded when work orders close, and that the variance parts of every close add up to its total. They also showed that the ledger postings of fiscal 2026 must be separated from the closing entry that clears the account. In the largest closes of the year, overhead makes up most of the variance. Which products carry it and how it grew from year to year are questions for Chapter 10.
